name: Prescott Statehood Tree

location.address: Yavapai County Courthouse Plaza, 120 S Cortez St, Prescott, AZ 86303 (northeast corner of the plaza, Gurley Street side)

official_register.name: Arizona's Magnificent Trees (Witness/Heritage Tree AZ0019 'Deodar Cedar', nominated by City of Prescott, 2011; also AZ0055 'Prescott Deodar Cedars', Heritage, 2002)

access: Free, open at any time: the Courthouse Plaza is a public square in the middle of downtown Prescott. Also the town's Christmas tree.
transport: On foot from anywhere downtown; Prescott has no rail; local Prescott Transit bus serves the Plaza area
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bronze plaque on a granite boulder at its foot, placed by Cub Scouts in 1960. It stands at the northeast corner of the Courthouse Plaza, on the Gurley Street side.
story:
Prescott cannot agree on when it planted its Statehood Tree, and the plaque at its foot may have the date wrong. The bronze plaque, set on a granite boulder by Prescott Cub Scouts in 1960, says the tree went in on 14 February 1912, the day Arizona became a state. The Sharlot Hall Museum disagrees. Its history column, citing the Journal Miner newspaper of June 1910, says a deodar cedar arrived by express from the Sierra Nevada that month and was planted on the Courthouse Plaza at a Fourth of July ceremony in 1910, and that the tree standing there today is that one.

Other accounts muddy it further. Arizona Highways credits Boy Scouts with a 1912 cedar. A Waymarking entry calls the tree a pine planted by the Masonic Lodge. The state's register of Arizona's magnificent trees lists it as a deodar cedar and a witness tree, standing when Arizona became a state. We give it as more than a century old, planted in 1910 or 1912.

Whichever year is right, it has stood at the corner of the plaza through the whole of Arizona's statehood. It is also the town's Christmas tree, lit each winter in front of the county courthouse.

It stands at the northeast corner of the plaza, on the Gurley Street side, free to visit at any hour.

name: Bicentennial Tree (Cortez Street oak)

location.address: 233 S Cortez St (east side, between S Goodwin St and W Carleton St), Prescott, AZ 86303

official_register.name: Arizona's Magnificent Trees (Witness/Heritage Tree AZ0020 'Arizona White Oak', nominated by City of Prescott, 2011; the register row has no address, so the match to this tree rests on the Courier calling it the centennial witness tree)

access: Free: stands on the public pavement edge of S Cortez Street next to the former City Hall site, currently behind protective fencing/netting during redevelopment (view from the street).
transport: On foot from the Courthouse Plaza, about 3 minutes
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the 1976 marker at its foot with a brass plate reading 'Arizona White Oak estimated 340 years old'. It stands on Cortez Street beside the old City Hall block.
story:
In 1976, as the United States turned 200, arborists recognised this oak as older than the country. A marker at its foot says the International Society of Arboriculture and the National Arborist Association honoured it that year as a tree that was alive in the time of the American Revolution. A brass plate added to the marker puts it at an estimated 340 years old.

That 1976 figure would make it nearly 390 today. Later press coverage gives 300, or more than 350. None of these is a ring count, so we give a range of roughly 300 to 360 years and keep it broad. Any of them makes it one of the oldest trees you can stand beside in downtown Prescott.

It is an Arizona white oak, a slow-growing native, and it has stood on this stretch of Cortez Street since long before there was a street, a town or a territory. The state's register of Arizona's magnificent trees lists an Arizona white oak in Prescott as a witness and heritage tree, which the local paper connects to this one. Locals call it the Bicentennial Tree, the Centennial Tree or the Revolutionary Tree.

The old City Hall block beside it is being redeveloped, and the oak stands behind protective fencing, so for now you look at it from the pavement.

name: Prescott Public Library oak

location.address: South of Prescott Public Library, 215 E Goodwin St, Prescott, AZ 86303 (southeast corner of the parking lot, reached from S Alarcon St)

access: Free, public: the oak stands in a small park area inside the library's public parking lot.
transport: On foot from the Courthouse Plaza, about 6 minutes
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one big oak in a small park area inside the library car park, in its southeast corner. A library history marker stands nearby.
story:
When Prescott built a car park here, it built it around an oak. A marker by the library says the city bought the property in 1998 and laid out the parking lot so the tree could stay, in a small park area of its own in the southeast corner.

The same marker gives the reason. The tree is an Arizona white oak, estimated to be over 300 years old, and the species grows slowly and may live to 500. That estimate is the marker's alone, and nobody has published a girth or a ring count, so take over 300 as the claim rather than a measurement.

If it is right, the oak was already old when Prescott was founded in the 1860s as the capital of the new Arizona Territory. It shares the age bracket with another Arizona white oak about 250 metres west on Cortez Street, which a 1976 marker calls 340 years old. Walking between the two takes a few minutes.

The city announced a rebuild of the lot in 2024. The oak is free to visit, reached from South Alarcon Street, and if you go, tell us how it came through the works.
